L14: The People’s Republic of China’s (PRC’s or China’s) ruling party, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP), is
L15: modernizing, reforming, and reorganizing its military, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), to defend the Party’s
L16: interests and meet defense requirements set by China’s leaders. These interests and defense requirements have
L17: expanded in recent decades as China’s economic and geopolitical power and ambitions have grown.
L18: The CCP’s national defense priorities include defending the Party; protecting what it views as China’s
L19: sovereignty, territorial integrity, and unity; protecting China’s growing overseas interests; deterring nuclear
L20: attacks and maintaining a nuclear counterattack capability; and deterring and countering acts it views as terrorism.
L21: Some of the Party’s national defense objectives, such as safeguarding the CCP’s control over the country and
L22: deterring nuclear attacks, have been in place for several decades. Others are more recent, such as safeguarding
L23: China’s overseas interests and its interests in space and cyberspace.
L24: China presents its military posture as purely defensive, serving only to protect China’s legitimate sovereign
L25: interests. It calls its national military strategy “active defense,” a concept that prescribes the ways in which China
L26: can defend its interests and prevail over a militarily superior adversary. This strategy allows for the use of
L27: offensive operational and tactical approaches, and the PLA has and continues to develop capabilities to wage
L28: offensive operations across a range of domains.
L29: China’s current military modernization push began in 1978 and accelerated in the 1990s. Xi Jinping, the General
L30: Secretary and “core leader” of the CCP, Chairman of the CCP’s Central Military Commission, and State
L31: President, has continued to make military modernization a priority and has linked military modernization to his
L32: signature issue: the “China Dream” of a modern, strong, and prosperous country. In 2017, Xi formalized three
L33: broad goals for the PLA: (1) to achieve mechanization of the armed forces and to make significant progress
L34: toward what the United States would call a “networked” force by 2020; (2) to “basically complete” China’s
L35: military modernization process by 2035; and (3) to have a “world-class” military by 2049, the centenary of the
L36: establishment of the PRC. Xi has initiated the most ambitious reform and reorganization of the PLA since the
L37: 1950s, in an effort to transform the military into a capable joint force as well as to further consolidate control of
L38: the PLA in the hands of Xi and the CCP.
L39: After decades of modernization supported by steady defense budget increases and other policies that promote
L40: military-technological advances, the PLA has become a formidable regional military with growing power
L41: projection capabilities. China’s armed forces are improving capabilities in every domain of warfare, have superior
L42: capabilities to other regional militaries in many areas, and are eroding U.S. military advantages in certain areas.
L43: China’s missile force, in particular, can put at risk a large range of targets in the region, including U.S. and allied
L44: bases. The PLA faces significant challenges and limitations, however, including a lack of combat experience,
L45: insufficient training in realistic combat scenarios, a limited ability to conduct joint operations, limited
L46: expeditionary capabilities, a new and largely untested organizational structure, and a dependence on foreign
L47: suppliers for certain military equipment and materials.

L94: Introduction
L95: The People’s Republic of China’s (PRC’s or China’s) ruling party, the Chinese Communist Party
L96: (CCP), has built itself a modern and regionally powerful military. Decades of military
L97: modernization have transformed the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) from a bloated, low-
L98: technology, ground forces-centric force to a leaner, more networked, high-technology force.1
L99: Increasingly capable across multiple warfare domains, the PLA has reached parity with the U.S.
L100: military in several areas and is strengthening its ability to “counter an intervention by an
L101: adversary in the Indo-Pacific region and project power globally,” according to the U.S.
L102: Department of Defense (DOD).2 Outside observers and the PLA itself also acknowledge that the
L103: PLA faces uncertainties and limitations, many of which the PLA is seeking to address, including
L104: through an ambitious reform and reorganization initiative begun in 2015.
L105: U.S. policymakers and observers increasingly describe China’s military buildup as a threat to
L106: U.S. and allied interests. This view reflects concerns about PLA capabilities—many of which
L107: appear designed specifically to counter U.S. military power—China’s growing economic and
L108: geopolitical power, and uncertainty about China’s regional and global intentions. Some Members
L109: of both parties in Congress have argued that meeting this perceived challenge requires the United
L110: States to strengthen its military advantages, and address major vulnerabilities, vis-à-vis China.
L111: Congressional decisions on this issue could shape, and be shaped by, U.S. defense strategy,
L112: budgets, plans, and programs, and the U.S. defense industrial base, among other things.
L113: This report discusses issues for Congress related to the PLA, the PLA’s ongoing reform and
L114: reorganization efforts, the PLA’s roles in advancing China’s national security interests, major
L115: features of China’s strategic outlook, PLA capabilities and modernization, uncertainties related to
L116: PLA capabilities, and the resources that fuel PLA modernization. In order to cover a wide range
L117: of topics in a concise format, the report does not go into great depth on some topics and omits
L118: other topics that might be considered germane.

L146: China’s military buildup as a threat to U.S. and allied interests. Top defense officials in the Trump
L147: and Biden administrations have identified China as the U.S. military’s “pacing threat.”3 This view

L153: strengthen its military advantages and address major vulnerabilities vis-à-vis China.

L155: reports, and defense bills.

L160: significant costs on the U.S. military in certain plausible scenarios. Observers continue to debate
L161: whether China could prevail in a regional conflict in the coming years.5
